rationale: A wins because it keeps the four pitch paths separated and turns missing evidence into reporting gates. "An unprofitable automaker turns its charging network into a revenue line" is a real business-desk story with unit-economics proof attached. B has usable bones, but "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" invents market behavior, and "The proprietary-charger era is fading" turns one company update into a trend verdict. A overreaches once, but B keeps selling conclusions it has not earned.
gaps_in_A: "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over" overstates the standards story. The update supports dual connectors on new stalls, not the end of a connector fight.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners" imports market context not in the supplied facts. Source it or cut it.
"so it is competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers" overreads "no partnership announced." Absence of an announced deal is not proof of a go-it-alone strategy.
gaps_in_B: "After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs" drags in an external peg the update did not provide. That is not grounding; that is a shortcut wearing a blazer.
"The proprietary-charger era is fading" is trend grandstanding. One Rivian announcement does not prove an era is ending.
"Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" invents a market reaction. No stock move, analyst note, or valuation evidence appears in the update.
"Rivian just became a charging-network operator" is sloppy. Rivian already operated the Adventure Network; the news is third-party access and premium pricing, not operator status.
